thesis: The 200-day moving average is not a statistical artifact -- it is a level thousands of participants mechanically watch and react to at the same time (managed-futures CTAs, trend-following mutual funds, and technically-oriented traders all use variants of it), so a break of it triggers correlated follow-on flow rather than random noise. The other side of the trade is supplied by participants who are slow or unwilling to move: index funds and 401k flows that buy/sell on a schedule unrelated to price level, and holders exhibiting the disposition effect who keep underwater positions past the point a trend-follower would already have exited, cushioning the trend-follower's fills. Applying the identical rule independently across three assets whose price drivers are structurally different (US equity beta, long-duration interest-rate risk, and a non-yielding hard asset with its own supply/demand book) means the three trend signals are not forced to fire together -- when equity trend breaks down in a genuine flight-to-quality event, rate or gold trend can still be up, which a single-asset or single-sector trend book cannot offer. This is not a hedge (the rules do not compare symbols to each other -- the engine cannot do that); it is three independent bets whose bad years are not the same years, which the correlation numbers in the memo support. What I expect to go wrong: fast V-shaped shocks. A 200-day average reacts on the order of weeks, not days, so a crash-and-snapback that completes inside a single quarter (COVID is the designed example) will be entered late on the way down and re-entered late on the way back up, capturing the worst of both transitions rather than avoiding them.
